vignette:
John has always prided himself on his handshake. For fifty years in industrial sales, a firm, confident handshake was his opening line, his closing argument, and his bond. Now, at seventy, he finds his hands are often damp and unsteady. He keeps them in his pockets more often than not, a gesture that feels as foreign to him as the persistent knot of anxiety in his stomach.

His life, until eight months ago, had been a testament to predictability and control. He and his wife, Carol, had their routines: coffee on the porch, his morning calls to prospects, her gardening, their shared dinner and an evening walk through their quiet suburban neighborhood. He was semi-retired but still kept a handful of his oldest, most lucrative accounts. He liked the work, the structure, the feeling of being useful. He felt he had earned this comfortable, controlled existence.

The control shattered on a Tuesday afternoon in the parking lot of a familiar grocery store. He was loading a case of water into his trunk when two young men approached. It happened so fast he barely had time to register their faces. One blocked his path while the other grabbed him from behind. The shove against the car knocked the wind out of him, the rough hands in his pockets were a profound violation. He felt a sharp, metallic pressure against his ribs. They took his wallet and, more painfully, the gold watch his company had given him for 30 years of service. The entire event lasted less than a minute, but the echo of his own helplessness has been deafening ever since.

In the first few weeks, John insisted he was fine. "Just a couple of punks," he'd tell Carol, waving off her concern. "I'm tougher than that." But his body betrayed him. The sound of running footsteps behind him on the sidewalk would cause his heart to hammer against his ribs. He started taking a different, longer route home from his office to avoid the part of town where the grocery store was. Soon, he was asking Carol to do all the shopping, claiming his back was sore.

Sleep became a battleground. He'd jolt awake in the dark, the phantom sensation of being grabbed still fresh on his skin, his pajamas soaked in a cold sweat. He stopped wanting to go out in the evenings. Their walks became a thing of the past. When Carol would suggest a movie or dinner with friends, he'd find an excuse. The world outside his front door had begun to feel menacing, unpredictable.

His work, once a source of pride, is now a source of dread. He finds himself scanning meeting rooms for exits, assessing every new face not for its potential as a client, but for its potential as a threat. During a recent presentation, a loud bang from a construction site outside sent a jolt of pure panic through him. He lost his train of thought completely, standing silent and flushed in front of a new customer, unable to recall what he was saying. He sees the pity and confusion in their eyes. He feels the shame of it like a physical weight.

He knows he's become irritable and distant. He snaps at Carol over small things-a misplaced set of keys, the volume on the television. He feels a chasm opening between them, but he doesn't know how to bridge it. How can he explain the shame of being an old man, so easily overpowered? He replays the assault in his mind, not with fear anymore, but with a relentless, critical eye. He tells himself he should have fought back, should have seen them coming, should have done *something*. The man with the firm handshake, the man who could close any deal and command any room, feels like a ghost. Now, all he feels is the ghost of a touch, a shove, and the unnerving lightness on his wrist where his watch used to be.
